These clusters will also be linked closely to private decision makers, such as employers, educational institutions, insurers, and hospitals. What controls over information collection and circulation will we have ready for these new public agencies?

If these judgments are valid, then we are now in a last-minute position to plan for the transition from one type of information theory of society to another. We must analyze the kinds of information our private and public agencies now collect, recognizing that increased possibilities of collation and circulation raise the danger potential of information our society was used to acquiring under the old information system.

This analysis would then take us to the planning and development of the new information system. The basic fact to be seen is that, even though machines in a carefully designed system can be made to do a great deal to protect privacy, man can defeat the most carefully designed system. This means that law and ethical restraints must be the final safeguards in the new information system.

What Do You Think?

Decades later, we still seem to find ourselves in a “last-minute position” with regard to the impact of information technologies. Why do you think privacy law has become more important in recent years? What developments have occurred to change the dynamics? How often in one day do you share personal information about yourself? Do you know who has access to that information? Should legal protection of personal information depend upon whether, and to what extent, you have shared that information with others?

As you read the following chapters, keep the “information as property” debate in mind because it is an important part of the “information dichotomy” that was introduced in this chapter. Some of the laws and cases that you will read concern efforts to protect information while others concern limitations on the protection of information. A property characterization is often used when a choice is made to protect information, but the benefits of information diffusion are stressed when limits are placed on the scope of protection. In many situations, the discussion of 29information as property or not property sets up a false dichotomy that fails to recognize that a property characterization tells us little about the scope of applicable rights and the circumstances under which created or collected information must be shared.

Notes

1.More on the property/not property debate. One reason that individuals and companies that possess information tend to like the property label is because of the rhetorical power of “theft.” These same individuals and companies also favor the natural rights and labor theories of property whereby the person who creates or collects information should be able to own and control it. Even if information was collected from public sources or received from others, these individuals and companies frequently argue that it is “their” information and that no one has a right to use it without their permission. But information law has never gone so far, and how far it should go is a question that is asked throughout this book.

As you will learn in Part II, all forms of information law include limitations on the scope of available protection, including the limitation that legal protection is not available for information that is generally known or otherwise “in the public domain.” Thus, even where compilations of information can be protected by law, including contract law, typically only the “new” (non-public) portions of those compilations are protected from tort or theft claims. Moreover, in addition to asking what information is protected by law (based upon a property theory or otherwise), we must ask the question: Protected from what? Typically, the right to rightfully acquire and read information and independently learn and reveal information is not restricted by law, but we might want to extend such protections to personal “private” information.

2.Be careful what you wish for. There are numerous consequences that flow from a property characterization that may not be favorable to the owner or recipient of information. For instance, an information owner, like DuPont, may be thrilled that its information is “property” when it seeks to recover damages for the theft of that information, but it would prefer that the same information not be treated as property for purposes of taxation. Similarly, the federal government may be thrilled to receive information about government fraud from a whistleblower, but not so thrilled when the whistleblower argues that the information was his “property” so that the tax rate on his payout should be taxed as capital gains instead of ordinary income. See e.g., Alderson v. United States, 718 F. Supp. 2d 1186 (2010). Also, there are responsibilities that can flow from ownership or possession of property, for instance the obligation to secure information or otherwise keep it confidential. When information is generally known or otherwise in the public domain, typically those obligations do not apply.

3.The public domain, information lockdown, and the access to knowledge movement. It is one thing to adopt laws and regulations that 30limit the scope of information protection, and quite another to ensure that individuals have affordable and meaningful access to the available body of information, whether in the public domain or not. To be able to access information it must be recorded, catalogued, and stored in ways that it can be found, obtained, and read. Historically in the United States, public libraries and public education have played an important role in the diffusion of information, but as information is being digitized, the costs of information access are increasing as more and more information is being controlled by private companies with a profit motive. At the same time, however, this digitalization (defined as the use of digital technologies to provide revenue) of information is making more information available over the internet, albeit at a price. Concerns about information lockdown, or what has been dubbed the “second enclosure movement,” have led to a counter movement collectively referred to as the “access to knowledge” (or A2K) movement which consists of efforts to ensure the low cost (and often free) availability of information. See Amy Kapczynski, The Access to Knowledge Mobilization and the New Politics of Intellectual Property, 117 Yale L. J. 804 (2008).

4.Bibliographic note. For more information about the topics discussed in this chapter, see: James Boyle, The Public Domain: Enclosing the Commons of the Mind (Yale University Press 2008); Lawrence Lessig, Free Culture (New York: Penguin, 2004); Anupam Chander, The New, New Property, 81 Tex. L. Rev. 715, 733–48 (2003); R. Polk Wagner, Information Wants to be Free: Intellectual Property and the Mythologies of Control, 103 Colum. L. Rev. 995 (2003); Jacqueline Lipton, Information Wants to be Property: Legal Commodification of E-Commerce Assets, 16 Int’l Rev./ L. Computers & Tech. 53 (2002); Lawrence Lessig, The Future of Ideas: The Fate of the Commons in a Connected World (New York: Random House, 2001); J.H. Reichman & Pamela Samuelson, Intellectual Property Rights in Data?, 50 Vand. L. Rev. 51 (1997); Andrew Beckerman-Rodau, Are Ideas Within the Traditional Definition of Property?: A Jurisprudential Analysis, 47 Ark. L. Rev. 603, 614–16 (1994); Wendy J. Gordon, On Owning Information: Intellectual Property and the Restitutionary Impulse, 78 Va. L. Rev. 149 (1992); Raymond T. Nimmer & Patricia Ann Krauthaus, Information as a Commodity: New Imperatives of Commercial Law, 55 Law & Contemp. Probs. 103, 113–14 (1992); Rochelle Cooper Dreyfuss, Information Products: A Challenge to Intellectual Property Theory, 20 N.Y.U. J. Int’l L. & Pol. 897 (1988).

31

Chapter 2

What Is “Information Law?”

■ ■ ■

Anticipated Learning Outcomes

At the conclusion of this chapter, students should be able to: define “information law” as a field of practice and study; identify the four modalities that are available to regulate, manage, and protect information, including their underlying theoretical bases; provide examples of how the four modalities often interact and their general relationship to “information governance.”

Problem to consider as you read this chapter:

Pretend you advise a real-world startup that seeks to be a social media platform that takes a protective (some might say, politically “progressive”) view of consumer privacy. It has three operating principles: “decentralization” (there is no one “central” computer system that holds all information); “freedom” (you can be pseudonymous or anonymous); and “privacy” (users own and can exercise control over their personal data). In its online Terms of Use (TOU) agreement, it explains: “You don’t sign over rights to a corporation or other interest who could use it.”

Since your client will be generating and handling a lot of information, how would you explain “information law” as a field to your client? How would you advise your client to use “information law” in its business model? Can it monetize the information it collects even if it claims not to own it?

A.Introduction

“Information law” as a discrete and coherent body of law does not exist. Rather, as you will learn throughout this book, there are a variety of laws and regulations governing the collection, management, protection, use, retention, and destruction of information. There are also laws and regulations governing the technological means (often referred to colloquially as “the pipes”) by which information is transmitted, stored, and shared, including through communication networks, computer systems, information processing technologies, and other “information, communications, and entertainment (ICE)” technologies. The laws governing ICE technologies include: media law, telecommunication law, and internet law, but even those fields of law often overlap with laws and 32regulations in other areas of what this text deems “information law.” Another area of overlap concerns the public’s interest in information, both in terms of information diffusion (including freedom of speech and the press) and access to information and knowledge.

Because information law has no accepted unitary definition and is not a discrete body of law, there is also no unifying theory of information law. But while the lack of a unitary definition and theory of information law may (at first) confuse or trouble you, it demonstrates the value of a course on information law. Because information law as a separate field of study and practice is under-theorized and not well understood, there is an immediate, practical need for a greater understanding of its contours and limitations. Increasingly, the bar demands that attorneys understand information as a field unto itself, much like one may think of contract or tort law.

This chapter’s primary purpose is to explain the various ways that information law can be defined and to introduce how the term “information law and governance” is used in this text. It will also elucidate the theoretical perspectives that might help the practicing lawyer, information professional, or budding scholar understand the scope and contours of information law. (Note that “information governance” is an important part of an information lawyer’s practice but is merely introduced in this chapter. It is the focus of many later chapters, especially those in Part III of this text.)

As further discussed below, some scholars were prescient in their predictions that information law, as a field, would come into its own. Nonetheless, they could not have predicted exactly how and when this would occur, what the scope of the field would become, or when lawyers and law professors would start paying attention. While many of the legal subjects covered in this book—including privacy law, trade secret law, internet law, and cyber-crimes—have long been the subject of law teaching, this book takes a more holistic approach that is consistent with the myriad information-related challenges facing businesses and their attorneys. In so doing, it presents a practical and integrated approach to information that sees the interconnectedness, and often inconsistencies, of the various areas of applicable law.

As a practical matter, this book also demonstrates that there is a dire and immediate need for lawyers who can translate complex information law and technology issues for meaningful consumption by clients, policymakers, consumers, and the public. This is due in large part to the increased scrutiny that is being paid to the information practices of many companies. For example, as Senator Richard Blumenthal said in the wake of Mark Zuckerberg’s testimony to Congress in April 2018 regarding Facebook’s information privacy practices: “There ought to be a law. There 33has to be a law. Unless there’s a law, [Facebook’s] business model is going to continue to maximize profit over privacy.” But while Congress may struggle to address questions of information privacy, a skilled information lawyer is equipped to craft laws and business practices that balance the legitimate interests of the public, private entities, government, and consumers.

Most legal problems, like whether information collection and use should be regulated, cannot be placed into one little box labeled with one area of law, but often require the application of multiple and overlapping legal principles. The ability of lawyers to see beyond one discrete field of law (for instance, tort or contract law) and look at the “bigger picture” is often what sets them apart from other professionals who have a more limited focus. It is certainly what sets the highly successful lawyers apart from average lawyers and is an essential skill to develop if one is to practice information law. As all successful lawyers know, finding solutions to legal problems requires careful consideration of many different factors, including: applicable law; the business goals of clients; risk assessment; and the likely costs and benefits of a given strategy.

But in our data and technology driven world, it also requires an understanding of potential technological solutions or, at the very least, the ability to effectively communicate with and understand computer and information technology (IT) experts. This does not mean that information lawyers must have computer science degrees or a background in coding. Rather, it means that information lawyers must be conversant in the languages used by those who seek solutions to legal problems through design and technology.

Indeed, sometimes practical or technical solutions are required, rather than purely legal solutions. Thus, to practice “information law” requires an understanding of this bigger picture in all its complexity. Attorneys and information professionals who are trained in information law can facilitate greater understanding among the various units of a client’s business. For instance, while information-related questions for IT professionals often concern where and how information flows and is secured, the questions for lawyers are likely to focus on whether and why information is collected, how it is being used, and where it is being stored and secured. Additionally, the information lawyer should have the skill to understand and navigate the complex relationship between the information-related needs of a company’s various constituencies.

As the foregoing quote by Senator Blumenthal reveals, a core aspect of information law is whether, how, and to what extent the collection and use of information should be regulated. More than ever before, society needs lawyers and others trained in information law and governance to help answer these questions and to assist clients to navigate an increasingly 34complex regulatory scheme, most recently with respect to privacy and cybersecurity. The following discussion of the varying definitions of information law, and the reasons why a body of information law exists and is needed, is the next step on our path toward understanding this important field of law.

B.Defining “Information Law”

Information professionals, such as librarians, archivists, records and information management (RIM) professionals, InfoSec professionals, and information scientists, can attest that the management, protection, and flow of information has long been of concern to businesses and governments. Entire colleges, schools, departments of universities, companies, and governmental institutions have been established to understand and manage the information that is created, collected, processed, stored, and discarded by businesses and governments. What is different today from twenty-five years ago is the magnitude of the information that businesses and governments must manage and the ways in which that information is collected and used. Today, information management has become less about storage and archiving and more about how information can be collected, accessed, and used to create value, and how risks associated with information can be reduced. It also is less about recording the past and more about using recorded information to predict the future, including by providing the data and analytics that are used in “artificial intelligence” (AI) and machine learning applications.

Given the sheer magnitude of information in modern society, and the many ways that information is collected and used, it is not surprising that various legal doctrines have developed to regulate information and that the definition of “information law” is unsettled and evolving. Over 30 years ago, Professor Peter Seipel argued that it is not even possible to identify information law in a singular, conclusive sense, and instead asserted that we should define the parameters of information law in terms of the overarching framework of law and “informatics,” that is, the information technologies field (i.e., the development and implementation of computer systems and networks). See Peter Seipel, Information Law Revisited, 7 J. Media L. & Prac. 51, 55 (1986). Signaling the need for the creation of an independent information law discipline, Professor Seipel presciently explained:

Thus, there exist at least two views of information law. One is associated primarily with data processing systems and decision making, with automation and data communications, with security and vulnerability aspects, and with the administration and marketing of information goods and services. The other view focuses on regulation of mass communications and places issues of freedom of expression, protection of privacy, copyright 35protection etc. in the foreground. Evidently, the two views share a number of interests, for example the interest in the regulation of technologies of communication and the protection of personal data.

Clearly, the two views are not mutually exclusive. Information law is not a narrow concept, neither is it associated with one single idea about the delimiting and structuring of the field. But information law as it may be developed within the framework of law and informatics seems to be both particularly challenging from the theoretical point of view and practically important with a view to our ability to control the information tools we now have at our disposal.

What Do You Think?

As you read this chapter, consider whether Professor Seipel’s description remains true today. What, if any, definitions of information law are particularly persuasive or unsatisfying? Based upon the materials in this chapter, how would you define “information law?”

In the 1990s and 2000s, others followed Seipel’s lead by focusing information law around its relationship to communications. For instance, Judge Willem F. Korthals Altes, in his edited volume Information Law Towards the 21st Century (1992), explained that “information law studies the communication processes in society as a whole.” Similarly, in his 2002 edition of Information Law in Practice, Professor Paul Marett set “wide” relational bounds on the term “to look at the law covering anything which is communicated, or is capable of communication, between human beings, or to from or between computers or other information-holding devices, or between such devices and humans.”

More recently, “information law” has come to be defined with respect to other laws. For instance, Harvard Law, in describing its Info/Law blog, describes information law as “an obvious convergence of intellectual property doctrine, communications regulation, First Amendment norms, and new technology.” Writing in a tongue-in-cheek fashion, it goes on to note that “hey, ‘information’ covers a lot of ground!” Similarly, the Institute for Information Law (IViR) at the University of Amsterdam defines information law to mean: “the law relating to the production, marketing, distribution, and use of information” that “cuts across traditional boundaries of legal research and teaching, comprising a wide set of legal issues at the crossroads of intellectual property, media law, telecommunications regulation, freedom of expression and information and right to privacy.”

If these are some common definitions of information law, what issues are animating and influencing them? Harkening back to Seipel’s insights, 36a recurring information law concern is the flow of information, including the regulation of the infrastructure through and by which information flows. New York University Law School’s Information Law Institute offers a typical example of how information law is often defined in relation to information flows. It describes itself as “an academic center for the study of law, policy, and social norms, defining and affecting the flow of information in a digitally networked society” (emphasis added). From this description, one may infer that information law can be defined as the way in which a combination of law, policy, and social norms defines and affects the flow and regulation of information. But what does information flow and regulation include, exactly?

Computer scientists, information scientists, and IT professionals have, since at least the dawn of World War II, been interested in information systems, information flows, and information management, with much of the focus being on how to develop computer systems that could more quickly and easily transmit, secure, and store information. Indeed, the technology that became the internet that we know today was developed as part of a military project (known as ARPANET) that began in the mid-1960s. But as Seipel noted, the technical aspects of information flows (i.e., informatics) should not be confused with the legal aspects, even as they are not mutually exclusive. One reason is because information need not exist in digital form or be transmitted electronically for it to be of concern to information professionals, their clients, or policymakers. Another reason is because, as noted in Chapter 1, there are different definitions, types, and uses of information.

One of the leading thinkers in early information law history, Professor Jon Bing, posited an information law “framework” that focused on data, information, and “communication channels.” See Jon Bing, Information Law: A Brief Introduction, 5 J. Media L. & Prac. 134–135 (1984). The appeal of this approach is that the policy issues with respect to the different types of information on one hand, and information flows on the other, are likely to be different.

In a 2003 law review article, Professor Jacqueline Lipton explored potential approaches to the regulation of information. She argued that information law should address three related concerns: property, privacy, and access. She asserted that these three elements are appropriate tools for an information law framework because “they all relate to control of various aspects of information.” Professor Lipton concluded that “creating a normative framework around the idea of rights to control and access to information is the key to creating a cohesive approach to information law and policy.” Jacqueline Lipton, A Framework for Information Law and Policy, 82 Or. L. Rev. 695, 722–723, 729 (2003) (emphasis added).

37

In a separate but related article, Mixed Metaphors in Cyberspace: Property in Information and Information Systems, 35 Loy. U. Chi. L.J. 235, 251 (2003), Lipton did not advocate for an absolute property right to information, but for a measured approach:

[I]t is futile to argue that legislatures should not continue to create information property rights. What is more important is to recognize that the market drives and will continue to drive, what is regarded as a property right. The appropriate role of the legislature should be to monitor and control the use of these rights. This role will include ensuring that the rights do not: (a) encroach to an unjustifiable extent on the public domain of information and ideas; (b) stifle invention, education, and creativity throughout society; and (c) interfere with privacy interests in relation to personal information.

As Professor Lipton suggests, identifying control, flow, and access as the central features of a cohesive information law framework raises the obvious next issue: Who should control, have access to, and be able to use information? As a practical matter, the answer often depends upon who possesses the information, but from a legal perspective it also depends upon whether the information is regulated and where and how it flows.

Questions of control and access highlight another core aspect of information law; namely, the public’s interest in information access and information flows (the focus of Chapters 3 and 10). Because humans need information to gain knowledge, spur invention and creativity, and participate in their communities, a variety of laws and public policies have long encouraged the creation, collection, and sharing of information. For instance, consider the establishment of public schools, universities, and libraries. All were designed to both add to the store of information and disseminate it widely. Two other examples are our patent and copyright laws which were designed (in varying degrees) to encourage the creation and disclosure of information.

When thinking about whether and how to regulate information, Professor Bing developed a potentially useful dichotomy. In Perspectives for the Development of Computers and Law and Computer Law: The Next 10 Years, 4 Journal of Law and Information Science 3, 17–18 (1993), he suggested “there are two main types of criteria used by the law to deal with information: One functional and one substantial,” as follows:

The functional perspective. Rules on creation abound. One important area, for instance is copyright law which assigns the exclusive right to exploit a work to the originator, the person creating the work. Rules of communication include both rules on confidentiality and the freedom of information legislation. Rules on storage would involve not only the data protection and 38computer security regulations, but also the legislation concerning the storage of accounts and related material for auditing, tax purposes etc. Even the law on libraries can be seen as a form of law governing the storage of information (or—in our characterisation of this concept—its representations, potential information or data). Rules on processing would include the law of evidence—what sort of information should be allowed to be passed on to a jury or the bench—as well as other regulations on procedures before courts, administrative bodies etc.

The substantial perspective. Rules relating to the content of information also abound—data protection legislation concerns personal data. There are restrictions related to blasphemy, slander, pornography, as well as regulations governing advertisements for alcoholic beverages, tobacco or medicines. The form may be relevant—the same information may be conveyed by a painting or a photograph, but different regulations apply. This seems rather obvious. Less obvious is using the structure of the representation of information as a criterion. But, for instance, in defining the type of personal data systems subject to data protection legislation one often refers to its structure—cf. the introductory example on the retrievability criterion in US and Norwegian law. Also the medium may be relevant—this is something different from both form and structure: Traditionally one distinguishes between the printed media and telemedia, but these may be subdivided. There are often special privileges and obligations for the publication of daily newspapers; broadcasting is typically subject to licensing schemes; telecommunication is closely regulated both with respect to the physical infrastructure and telecommunication services. The recent directives of the European Community to secure competition within this area may be an exponent of these regulations.

Professor Bing went on to explain: “I]t will not be appropriate to include all these aspects within computers and law. On the other hand, all these regulations concern in one way or the other information, and this implies that information technology has a potential impact on all these regulations.” Id. at 18.

What Do You Think?

The foregoing suggests that we need a comprehensive approach to the collection, storage, and use of information, but what might that framework look like? Should it apply to all information, or just some? How might the regulation of any body of information affect its flow and our access to it?
39

Faced with the above dynamic issues, it should be no surprise that the very parameters of information law are yet to be stabilized, even as some have attempted to identify its metes and bounds. However, we can all agree (and the authors of this book concur) that information law covers much ground and much of it must be considered when thinking about information regulation and governance. As used in this text, “information law” concerns the laws that govern how information (broadly defined) is created, collected, organized, protected, secured, accessed, shared, transmitted, used, and discarded, primarily by businesses and governments. It also concerns related public policy issues that should inform policymaking, primarily the public interests in information access, diffusion, and transparency and each of our individual interests in information privacy.

This text seeks to apply the above definition both theoretically and practically. Like pioneering information law scholar Raymond Nimmer’s seminal treatise, Information Law, it brings together previously disparate areas of law, from trade secrecy (introduced in DuPont v. Christopher in Chapter 1) to the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) and privacy, to government transparency; all to teach the interconnectedness of the various areas of law that relate to information. But knowing what the applicable laws are and understanding why they exist are two different things, as the next section of this chapter illuminates.

C.Information Theory and Methods for Regulating Information

It is one thing to define what “information” and “information law” is, and quite another to determine how best to regulate the creation, collection, use, and flow of information. The immediate question, discussed below, is: what levers, in addition to law, can and are used to govern information? This is an important question to ask because, as you will learn in Part III, the practice of information law and governance is not just about the use and application of applicable law. The creation, collection, use, and flow of information can also be controlled using self-help in the form of private ordering, technology, and social norms. The use of these sorts of private measures, in turn, raises important issues concerning the public’s ability to access, learn from, and use information.

In the following excerpt from his article, The Law of the Horse: What Cyberlaw Might Teach, Professor Larry Lessig identifies four modalities of regulation that, when you think about it, are broadly applicable to every legal problem that lawyers encounter.

40

What Do You Think?

As you read the following, consider how governments, individuals, and businesses, might use one or more of the listed modalities to regulate the creation, collection, use, flow, access, and dissemination of information. Also consider how you might use each modality to manage and protect the information held by or owned by your clients.

The Law of the Horse: What Cyberlaw Might Teach

Lawrence Lessig
113 Harv. L. Rev. 501, 507–508 (1999)

Behavior, we might say, is regulated by four kinds of constraints. Law is just one of those constraints. Law (in at least one of its aspects) orders people to behave in certain ways; it threatens punishment if they do not obey. The law tells me not to buy certain drugs, not to sell cigarettes without a license, and not to trade across international borders without first filing a customs form. It promises strict punishments if these orders are not followed. In this way, we say that law regulates.

But not only law regulates in this sense. Social norms do as well. Norms control where I can smoke; they affect how I behave with members of the opposite sex; they limit what I may wear; they influence whether I will pay my taxes. Like law, norms regulate by threatening punishment ex post. But unlike law, the punishments of norms are not centralized. Norms are enforced (if at all) by a community, not by a government. In this way, norms constrain, and therefore regulate.

Markets, too, regulate. They regulate by price. The price of gasoline limits the amount one drives—more so in Europe than in the United States. The price of subway tickets affects the use of public transportation—more so in Europe than in the United States. Of course, the market is able to constrain in this manner only because of other constraints of law and social norms: property and contract law govern markets; markets operate within the domain permitted by social norms. But given these norms, and given this law, the market presents another set of constraints on individual and collective behavior.

And finally, there is a fourth feature of real space that regulates behavior—“architecture.” By “architecture” I mean the physical world as we find it, even if “as we find it” is simply how it has already been made. That a highway divides two neighborhoods limits the extent to which the neighborhoods integrate. That a town has a square, easily accessible with a diversity of shops, increases the integration of residents in that town. That Paris has large boulevards limits the ability of revolutionaries to protest. That the Constitutional Court in Germany is in Karlsruhe, while the capital is in Berlin, limits the influence of one branch of government over the other.

41

These constraints function in a way that shapes behavior. In this way, they too regulate.

These four modalities regulate together. The “net regulation” of any particular policy is the sum of the regulatory effects of the four modalities together. A policy trades off among these four regulatory tools. It selects its tool depending upon what works best.

What Do You Think?

Are there one or more modalities of the four listed above that seem better suited for the creation, protection, diffusion, and control of information? What would it depend upon? What else would you want to know?

Below we explore each of the four modalities of regulation identified by Professor Lessig and how they are used to regulate information (although as Professor Lessig notes, all the modalities interact in important ways). For instance, most legal systems are highly dependent upon individuals and businesses voluntarily agreeing to follow the law and the social pressure that is often brought to bear to make sure laws are followed. In his book, Why People Obey the Law, Professor Tom R. Tyler explained that: “[i]f people view compliance with the law as appropriate because of their attitudes about how they should behave, they will voluntarily assume the obligations to follow the rules.” Similarly, while architectural features like locked file cabinets and secure networks can be designed to protect information, the success of these measures depends a great deal on whether it is socially acceptable to try to circumvent them, and whether their features can be easily changed or altered.

1.Social Norms and Information

According to the Oxford Dictionary of Sociology, “social norms are informal understandings that govern the behavior of a society.” In Sociology: Exploring the Architecture of Everyday Life, David M. Newman defines a norm as a “culturally defined standard or rule of conduct.” Norms can develop and exist in small groups of people, such as a family, or in larger groups such as a business, an industry, or a town. Generally, they represent the values, customs, and traditions of the group and are enforced by the group. Sometimes they exist alone, or supplement other regulatory modalities. For example, it is technically illegal for individuals to access someone else’s mail after it has been placed in their mailbox by the U.S. Postal Service, but even without such a law, most people respect the sanctity of their neighbor’s mailbox.

In a country like the United States that values education, free enterprise, and freedom of speech, it is not surprising that there are limited social constraints on the free flow of publicly available information and the acquisition of knowledge. Twitter and Facebook abound with free flowing 42(but not necessarily unprotected) information. But while we are generally free to peruse social media or pick up a book or newspaper and read it, and are encouraged to do so throughout our lives, social norms also dictate that certain information is generally off-limits. Personal information about one’s health and wealth and details of intimate social interactions are some examples of the types of information that we usually do not share freely. However, as anyone who uses Facebook, Twitter, or Instagram knows, the information norms that we follow in one context are not always followed in other contexts. For example, we might be reluctant to tell the details of a date to our grandmother, but we will post photos of the date for all our Instagram followers to see.

Understanding the role of social norms as a form of regulation is essential for an understanding of information law more broadly, particularly with respect to the norms that exist among the creators, collectors, and users of information. John Seely Brown and Professor Paul Duguid addressed information as a social construct in their prescient book, The Social Life of Information, published in 2002, as the internet was coming into its own as an economic and social force. As you read the excerpt below from their chapter titled “Learning—In Theory and in Practice,” recall Chapter 1’s discussion of the difference between “information,” “data,” and “knowledge” and consider the role of humans in the use and management of information. What do Brown and Duguid say about social norms in the context of “information governance” (or, as they call it, “knowledge management”), and the role of people in the “knowledge economy?” Do you agree with them?

What Do You Think?

How can understanding the social norms of a group (e.g. computer hackers and crackers) assist government regulators, information lawyers, and information professionals to better address information-related problems? What if applicable law assumes the existence of certain social norms, but those norms do not exist in all communities? Can laws, alone, change social norms?

The Social Life of Information

John Seely Brown and Paul Duguid
Harvard University Press 119–122 (2002)

People are increasingly eager that their perfectly respectable cache of information be given the cachet of knowledge. Such redefinitions surreptitiously extend the overlapping area where knowledge and information appear as interchangeable terms.

43

Nevertheless, if we check the language of knowledge management at the door, there do appear to be some generally accepted distinctions between knowledge and information. Three strike us as particularly interesting.

First, knowledge usually entails a knower. That is, where people treat information as independent and more-or-less self-sufficient, they seem more inclined to associate knowledge with someone. In general, it sounds right to ask, “Where is that information?” but odd to ask, “Where’s that knowledge?” as if knowledge normally lay around waiting to be picked up. It seems more reasonable to ask, “Who knows that?”

Second, given this personal attachment, knowledge appears harder to detach than information. People treat information as a self-contained substance. It is something that people pick up, possess, pass around, put in a database, lose, find, write down, accumulate, count, compare, and so forth. Knowledge, by contrast, doesn’t take as kindly to ideas of shipping, receiving, and quantification. It is hard to pick up and hard to transfer. You might expect, for example, someone to send you or point you to the information they have, but not to the knowledge they have.

Third, one reason knowledge may be so hard to give and receive is that knowledge seems to require more by way of assimilation. Knowledge is something we digest rather than merely hold. It entails the knower’s understanding and some degree of commitment. Thus, while one person often has conflicting information, he or she will not usually have conflicting knowledge. And while it seems quite reasonable to say, “I’ve got the information, but I don’t understand it,” it seems less reasonable to say, “I know, but I don’t understand,” or “I have the knowledge, but I can’t see what it means.” (Indeed, while conventional uses of information don’t necessarily coincide with the specialist uses, as we noted earlier, “information theory” holds information to be independent of meaning.)

WHERE IS THE KNOWER LOST IN THE INFORMATION?

Knowledge’s personal attributes suggest that the shift toward knowledge may (or should) represent a shift toward people. Focusing on process, as we argued, draws attention away from people, concentrating instead on disembodied processes and the information that drives them. Focusing on knowledge, by contrast, turns attention toward knowers. Increasingly, as the abundance of information overwhelms us all, we need not simply more information, but people to assimilate, understand, and make sense of it.

The markets of the knowledge economy suggest that this shift is already underway. Investment is no longer drawn, as postindustrial champions like to point out, to bricks and mortar and other forms of fixed capital. Nor does it pursue income streams. (In some of the newest knowledge organizations there is as yet barely enough income to puddle, let alone stream.) Instead, investors see value in people and their know-how—people 44with the ability to envisage and execute adventurous new business plans and to keep re-envisaging these to stay ahead of the competition.

So, while the modern world often appears increasingly impersonal, in those areas where knowledge really counts, people count more than ever. In this way, a true knowledge economy should distinguish itself not only from the industrial economy but also from an information economy. For though its champions like to present these two as distinct, the information economy, like the industrial economy, shows a marked indifference to people. The industrial economy, for example, treated them en masse as interchangeable parts—the factory “hands” of the nineteenth century. The information economy threatens to treat them as more or less interchangeable consumers and processors of information. Attending to knowledge, by contrast, returns attention to people, what they know, how they come to know it, and how they differ.

The importance of people as creators and carriers of knowledge is forcing organizations to realize that knowledge lies less in its databases than in its people. It’s been said, for example, that if NASA wanted to go to the moon again, it would have to start from scratch, having lost not the data, but the human expertise that took it there the last time. Similarly, Tom Davenport and Larry Prusak argue that when Ford wanted to build on the success of the Taurus, the company found that the essence of that success had been lost with the loss of the people that created it. Their knowledge was not stored in information technologies. It left when they left.

* * *

* * * In all, the job of knowledge management cannot involve just the protection and exploitation of patents. It must include the cultivation of knowledgeable workers. Focusing on information, however, makes this kind of cultivation difficult.

———

If Brown and Duguid are right, people remain at the center of information (or knowledge) governance, even in the face of technological advancement (which is even more pronounced today given the advent of artificial intelligence and machine learning, where laws and policy analysis lag-behind the implementation of these technologies in society). Therefore, the practice of information law and governance must be as much about the management of people and their norms as it is about the management of information and related technologies, including the people who use information to program computerized systems and robots. In fact, it is well-known in the InfoSec community that the ability of computer hackers (and crackers) to employ social engineering techniques is the greatest risk to information security, principally because humans are fallible and can be manipulated.

45

What Do You Think?

How does one apply the distinction between knowledge and information to the practice of information law? How important are the rights of employees and the public’s interest in information and knowledge to the analysis? Should information law inform human resource managers, and if so, how?

Consider the issues surrounding whether to share information. In the practice of law and in the field of information governance, it is important to understand that all businesses and industries have norms related to the creation, collection, use, retention, sharing, and management of information. This includes, for example, the human resources department of businesses. Some of these norms may be underdeveloped and a matter of happenstance, often existing without consideration of the importance of a given type of information. Other times these norms are sophisticated and intentional, either because a business sees the need to zealously guard the information it possesses (such as the formula for Coca-Cola) or because it derives value from sharing and licensing information. Thus, to provide clients appropriate advice concerning the information they possess or control, it is necessary to learn and understand the applicable norms of a clients’ business, its employees, and the industry in which it operates. Only then can you help your clients to implement an information governance strategy that meets their needs.

With respect to the protection of information, there is a range of possible approaches that we label collectively as the “information protection continuum.” On one end of the information protection continuum is the “open innovation” or “open source” model where individuals and companies choose to voluntarily share information at no or low cost; not, necessarily, because they do not value the information that they share, but because they value the sharing and disclosure of information more so than its protection. On the other end of the spectrum is the “closed” or “proprietary” model where individuals and companies zealously protect their information and refuse to share it, except possibly under very limited and stringent circumstances. In between are individuals and companies that release some types of information, but guard other types. Additionally, sometimes various practical, personal, social, and legal requirements will demand that information be shared, even if it is the type of information that would otherwise be treated as “private” or “secret.” For instance, regulated companies are often required to share confidential information with government regulators.

Consider the published comments and policies of the following industry leaders with respect to information that their companies possess:

46

Elon Musk, June 12, 2014

Yesterday, there was a wall of Tesla patents in the lobby of our Palo Alto headquarters. That is no longer the case. They have been removed, in the spirit of the open source movement, for the advancement of electric vehicle technology.

Tesla Motors was created to accelerate the advent of sustainable transport. If we clear a path to the creation of compelling electric vehicles, but then lay intellectual property landmines behind us to inhibit others, we are acting in a manner contrary to that goal. Tesla will not initiate patent lawsuits against anyone who, in good faith, wants to use our technology.

* * *

We believe that Tesla, other companies making electric cars, and the world would all benefit from a common, rapidly-evolving technology platform.

Technology leadership is not defined by patents, which history has repeatedly shown to be small protection indeed against a determined competitor, but rather by the ability of a company to attract and motivate the world’s most talented engineers. We believe that applying the open source philosophy to our patents will strengthen rather than diminish Tesla’s position in this regard.

Dupont’s Code of Conduct, January 2017

It is critical that all employees protect company information that has not been made public. Non-public information that has economic value to the company is “trade secret” information. Examples of company trade secret information include the following when not public: business plans, pricing and cost information, research and development plans and strategies, research data and inventions, product formulas and ingredients, process and design information. “Inside information,” . . . is another example of non-public, confidential information that must not be shared with others without specific authorization.

———

On the surface, the two quotes above represent diametrically opposed views on the issue of information sharing that reflect the relative maturity of the two industries in which the companies operate, but with each approach being selected to improve the success of each company and with each company acknowledging the existence of information in the public sphere. But when one digs deeper, there are more similarities between the two approaches than might immediately be understood. Although Elon Musk decided that Tesla will “freely” share its electric vehicle technology—primarily to speed-up the development of an electric car industry which Tesla hopes to lead—there is still plenty of information that Tesla has chosen to protect, mainly in the form of information that is not disclosed in 47its patents (which are often called “trade secrets”). Conversely, although DuPont takes a hardline with its employees to protect its trade secrets, it also acknowledges that there are limits on what it can protect and that there may be circumstances where the sharing or disclosure of its trade secrets would be authorized.

Beyond the views of individual companies, there are norms in various industries and contexts that require more or less protection for information, depending upon the need to facilitate the sharing of information. Often, the more mature an industry is, the more inclined companies operating in that industry will be to adopt a proprietary model of information sharing, but the type of information involved also dictates applicable norms. For example, in the publishing industry, the norm is for authors (actual and aspiring) to submit their ideas for new books without first obtaining an express promise of confidentiality. While to an unsophisticated lawyer this may seem like a risky approach, it generally works to protect book ideas for three reasons: (1) the publishers follow a well-established professional norm not to disclose or use submitted ideas without permission of the author; (2) the flow of ideas from authors would decrease if publishers were known to use or disclose submitted ideas without compensation; and (3) usually, the ideas are submitted in the form of a completed (or nearly complete) manuscript which, pursuant to copyright law, protects the author’s particular expression of the idea.

Similar norms of confidentiality exist among venture capitalists with respect to new inventions or ideas for new business ventures. As the television show Shark Tank reveals, pitches to venture capitalists are typically made without any express promise of confidentiality; however, the norms of venture capitalists (designed to encourage pitches) make it unlikely that the disclosed ideas will be used without compensation. Thus, although a breach of the norms is possible, they are relatively rare, particularly if the person who is making the pitch has already secured some intellectual property protection for her idea.

Related to the information protection continuum is the fact that some individuals, companies, and industries, either with respect to discrete types of information or in connection with general business practices, consciously choose to follow a policy of “open innovation.” Popularized by Henry Chesbrough in his book, Open Innovation: The New Imperative for Creating and Profiting from Technology, the central idea behind an open innovation policy is that some companies and industries have more to gain from taking advantage of widely-distributed and shared information because it is more efficient and faster to learn from others instead of having to invest in research and development. Thus, many technology competitions and “pitch competitions” are specifically (although often not transparently) designed to generate and capture the ideas of those who enter the competitions.

48

Others identify great social value in freely sharing information about their inventions. This approach is at the heart of the quote by Elon Musk, above. It also motivated many famous inventors to dedicate their inventions to the world, including: Benjamin Franklin, who chose not to patent the Franklin Stove; Jonas Salk, who freely shared the information he discovered about the Polio vaccine he invented; and Tim Berners-Lee, who invented the “World Wide Web” and freely distributed it to the world. In fact, a recent study of how startups use information underscores the fact that not only does an open innovation norm lead to social value, but the very sharing of the fact that an innovation exists can lead to financial investment by third parties. See David S. Levine & Ted Sichelman, Why Do Startups Use Trade Secrets?, 94 Notre Dame L. Rev. 751 (2018). This is why, for instance, patent and trade secret portfolios are important to many businesses, even if the value of the underlying inventions and information is unknown; they signal value and attract investments.

Given the possibility of varying industry and company norms, a granular and flexible application of information law principles is often needed to achieve the optimal result for the interested parties. A particular set of social norms that should be considered when assisting a client to protect its information relates to the decision to create, collect, and maintain information in the first place. As you will learn in later chapters, some laws dictate the types of information that must and can be maintained by individuals and businesses and some laws either limit the collection of information or establish rules for the handling of collected information. But in the absence of such laws, it is the specific requirements of a business and applicable norms that should dictate the information that a business creates, collects, maintains, uses, and discards. Sometimes, a business may think it needs to collect or maintain information, but other times the value of information to a business is outweighed by the risks that the information poses to the business.

With increased talk of the value of data, data analytics, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, and knowledge management, many businesses have gotten into the habit of collecting and digitizing information without first considering the types of information they need to create, collect, and maintain or whether they are deriving any benefit from that information (more on this topic in Chapter 12). For example, many individuals and companies conduct business with a variety of vendors but they do not necessarily need to collect and maintain detailed information about those vendors. (Have you recorded the address and phone number of your neighborhood market?) Similarly, although an online retailer has an interest in keeping and maintaining certain information about its customers, principally because the retailer wants to send advertisements to those customers, it does not need to keep every bit of information that it may learn about a customer. First, such a practice can be creepy and off-49putting to consumers. Second, it may expose the company to legal requirements associated with the collected information or, worse, liability for the failure to protect the information.

It is also important for lawyers and information professionals to understand how social norms develop and how they can help their clients to identify risks and facilitate the establishment of desired information-related norms and practices. For example, if a culture of confidentiality is desired, merely requiring all employees to sign a confidentiality agreement (also known as a non-disclosure agreement or NDA, see Chapter 4) is probably not enough to create the desired culture. Frequent repetition and education about the expectation of confidentiality and its parameters is also needed. Leadership and top-level compliance with the desired information norms and practices is also required, as lower level employees are bound to take cues from their superiors. Additionally, because individuals are disinclined to follow social norms that are perceived to be illogical, unfair, inconsistent, or overly complicated, businesses should take care not to overreach in their assertion of the need for confidentiality. Not all information is protected by law, so the assertion of norms to protect all information is likely to be viewed with skepticism and will fail to educate employees about which information is truly important.

2.Markets and Information

The term “market” has a variety of definitions depending upon the context in which it is used. For example, in the advertising world, it refers to the organizations and individuals that are likely to be interested in a particular good or service. For present purposes, and as used by Professor Lessig above, the term is used broadly and generally to refer to the place where sellers and buyers interact in the exchange of goods and services. This “place” can be a physical market, like a grocery store, or a virtual market, like the internet. It also includes the numerous transactions that occur between individuals and businesses, often through the exchange of promises evidenced by implied or express contracts. As you will read below, Professor Manuel Castells might define a market broadly as a “network,” but usually markets facilitate a transaction of some sort, be it between individuals, companies, or robots.

If we truly live in an Information Age made up of intersecting networks, then it is easy to see how there can be markets in information that regulate informational behavior. In a free market economy, where information can flow unencumbered, such regulation is typically a simple matter of supply and demand. Generally, the more information on a particular topic that is freely available, the less value that information has in the hands of an individual or company, and the less likely more of the same information will be supplied. For example, due to the availability of Wikipedia, you may conclude that you need not purchase a set of 50encyclopedias. As a result, fewer companies are willing to publish encyclopedias. On the other hand, if valued information is collected and made accessible through subscription services, like Amazon and Netflix, then more companies will be willing to distribute information but at a price that is beyond the means of some. We are beginning to see this with respect to the creation and distribution of television programming, which once was only provided for free over public airwaves but now comes at an ever-increasing cost.

Additionally, there are reasons why there might be a healthy market in even widely-distributed information. First, there is often value in having information earlier rather than later. For example, although you could drive to your local hall of records to research the ownership of a piece of real property, it may be easier and more convenient to subscribe to a database that provides that information over the internet. In such a case, although it seems that you are seeking information, you are actually seeking convenience. Thus, one could argue that the value of the database is not the information it contains, but the way that the information is presented and made available. Similarly, if the information at issue is valuable due to its secrecy, early access to it can lead to what is known as a “first mover advantage;” the frequently touted (but not always applicable) ability of the first entrant in a market segment to gain an advantage over future competitors.

A market for widely-distributed information can also be created by adding additional or different content. For example, the database of real estate records might include a search function that allows users to quickly search the records of similar or nearby properties, or that shows other properties owned by the same owner. In the case of encyclopedias, the value-added may lie in the veracity of the information it conveys and the citation to reliable sources it provides. (Which is why Encyclopedia Britannica continues to exist despite the advent of Wikipedia.) A market for widely-distributed information can also be created based upon the way the information is presented, explaining why some non-fiction works are more popular than others. As the business models of many online companies reveal, markets in widely-distributed information can also be created for the advertising revenues they generate, particularly if the data that such companies collect allow for targeted marketing.

The regulation of search engines and databases, or lack thereof, is discussed later in this book and constitutes the prime example of modern information access and its parameters. For now, consider the theoretical and practical problems with using markets to regulate behavior related to information, including the market’s relationship to other levers of regulation, particularly architecture. If businesses can be created based principally upon the information that they collect, secure, and use (including as raw material for increasingly sophisticated artificial 51intelligence and machine learning applications) and the networks they control, how can companies without access to the same information and networks even compete? As further discussed below, there are three principal issues: (1) the inclusiveness of markets, or lack thereof; (2) the free-rider problem; and (3) Arrow’s Information (or disclosure) Paradox.

What Do You Think?

As you read the excerpt that follows, consider how markets as a mode of regulation might be limited by the structural barriers associated with becoming a part of our modern information ecosystem. What if you do not own a computer or the requisite software that would allow you to access information? Or, what if the only way to access information is through an app and you do not agree with the “permissions” that the app requires? Have you ever been forced to download an app you didn’t like merely to complete a commercial transaction?

Communication Power

Manuel Castells

Oxford University Press 24–27 (2009)
© 2009 Manuel Castells
Reproduced with permission of Oxford University Press through PLSclear

The Global Network Society

A network society is a society whose social structure is made around networks activated by microelectronics-based, digitally processed information and communication technologies. I understand social structures to be the organizational arrangements of humans in relationships of production, consumption, reproduction, experience, and power expressed in meaningful communication coded by culture.

Digital networks are global, as they have the capacity to reconfigure themselves, as directed by their programmers, transcending territorial and institutional boundaries through telecommunicated computer networks. So, a social structure whose infrastructure is based on digital networks has the potential capacity to be global. However, network technology and networking organization are only means to enact the trends inscribed in the social structure. The contemporary process of globalization has its origin in economic, political, and cultural factors, as documented by scholarly analyses of globalization. But, as a number of studies have indicated, the forces driving globalization could only be effectuated because they have at their disposal the global networking capacity provided by digital communication technologies and information systems, including computerized, long-haul, fast, transportation networks. This is, in fact, what separates, in size, speed, and complexity, the current process of globalization from previous forms of globalization in earlier historical periods.

52

Thus, the network society is a global society. However, this does not mean that people everywhere are included in these networks. For the time being, most are not. But everybody is affected by the processes that take place in the global networks that constitute the social structure. The core activities that shape and control human life in every corner of the planet are organized in global networks: financial markets; transnational production, management, and the distribution of goods and services; highly skilled labor; science and technology, including higher education; the mass media; the Internet networks of interactive, multipurpose communication; culture; art; entertainment; sports; international institutions managing the global economy and intergovernmental relations; religion; the criminal economy; and the transnational NGOs and social movements that assert the rights and values of new, global civil society. Globalization is better understood as the networking of these socially decisive global networks. Therefore, exclusion from these networks, often in a cumulative process of exclusion, is tantamount to structural marginalization in the global network society.

The network society diffuses selectivity throughout the planet, working on the pre-existing sites, cultures, organizations, and institutions that still make up most of the material environment of people’s lives. The social structure is global, but most of the human experience is local, both in territorial and cultural terms. Specific societies, as defined by the current boundaries of nation-states, or by the cultural boundaries of their historical identities, are deeply fragmented by the double logic of inclusion and exclusion in the global networks that structure production, consumption, communication, and power. I propose the hypothesis that this fragmentation of societies between the included and the excluded is more than the expression of the time-lag required by the gradual incorporation of previous social forms into the new dominant logic. It is, in fact, a structural feature of the global network society. This is because the reconfiguring capacity inscribed in the process of networking allows the programs governing every network to search for valuable additions everywhere and to incorporate them, while bypassing and excluding those territories, activities, and people that have little or no value for the performance of the tasks assigned to the network. * * *

The network society works on the basis of binary logic of inclusion/exclusion, whose boundaries change over time, both with the changes in the networks’ programs and with the conditions of performance of these programs. It also depends on the ability of social actors, in various contexts, to act on these programs, modifying them in the direction of their interests. The global network society is a dynamic structure that is highly malleable to social forces, to culture, to politics, and to economic strategies. But what remains in all instances is its dominance over activities and people who are external to the networks. In this sense, the global 53overwhelms the local—unless the local becomes connected to the global as a node in alternative global networks constructed by social movements.

Thus, the uneven globalization of the network society is, in fact, a highly significant feature of its social structure. The coexistence of the network society, as global structure, with industrial, rural, communal, or survival societies, characterizes the reality of all countries, albeit with different shares of population and territory on both sides of the divide, depending on the relevance of each segment for the dominant logic of each network. This is to say that various networks will have different geometries and geographies of inclusion and exclusion: the map of the global criminal economy is not the same as the map resulting from the international location patterns of high-technology industry.

In theoretical terms, the network society must be analyzed, first, as a global architecture of self-reconfiguring networks constantly programmed and reprogrammed by the powers that be in each dimension; second, as the result of the interaction between the various geometries and geographies of the networks that include core activities—that is, the activities shaping life and work in society; and, third, as the result of a second-order interaction between these dominant networks and the geometry and geography of the disconnection of social formations left outside the global networking logic.

The understanding of power relationships in our world must be specific to this particular society. An informed discussion of this specificity requires a characterization of the network society in its main components: production and appropriation of value, work, communication, culture, and its mode of existence as a spatiotemporal formation.

What Do You Think?

Are you convinced that our information ecosystem mirrors the problems associated with societal “haves” and “have-nots,” from educational opportunity to food scarcity? Is exclusion a design feature of the modern information network society? If so, what are its ramifications in the marketplace and how might it be regulated?

If information markets are or can be inclusive—which, as Professor Castells argues, is a big “if”—there are two other related problems. The first is the free-rider problem which posits that individuals and companies will consume more goods and services when they do not have to pay for them, creating a market failure. Related to information, the argument goes: individuals and companies that go to the time, trouble, and expense to develop or collect information and knowledge through research and development (R&D) efforts or otherwise will be less inclined to invest in those efforts or share their information if the information can be freely used 54once it is disclosed to the public. Thus, the potential availability of information is diminished.

In the absence of laws, the owner of information might resort to self-help and carefully guard its information by refusing to share it with anyone. But while this solves the free-rider problem, it gives rise to another problem, known as “Arrow’s Information (or Disclosure) Paradox,” named after Kenneth Arrow, whose 1962 paper introduced the concept. See excerpt, below. The paradox is that the holder of information will be reluctant to share it due to the free-rider problem, but the prospective purchaser (or licensee) of the information will be reluctant to purchase the information sight unseen. This results in a transactional stalemate (a market failure) because the needs of the prospective purchaser are not being met and, as a result, the information owner cannot reap full-value from its information. This scenario can arise, for example, in licensing negotiations where information must be shared for parties to assess the merits of the transaction and is one of the justifications for intellectual property (IP) laws.

Economic Welfare and the Allocation of Resources for Invention

Kenneth J. Arrow
The Rate and Direction of Inventive Activity: Economic and Social Factors
Universities-National Bureau Committee for Economic Research, Committee on Economic Growth of the Social Science Research Council
Princeton University Press (1962), pp. 614–615

It might be expected that information will be traded in, and of course to a considerable extent this is the case, as is illustrated by the numerous economic institutions for transmission of information, such as newspapers. . . . In the absence of special legal protection, the [information] owner cannot, however, simply sell information on the open market. Any one purchaser can destroy the monopoly, since he can reproduce the information at little or no cost. Thus the only effective monopoly would be the use of the information by the original possessor. This, however, will not only be socially inefficient, but also may not be of much use to the owner of the information either, since he may not be able to exploit it as effectively as others. With suitable legal measures, information may become an appropriable commodity. Then the monopoly power can indeed be exerted. However, no amount of legal protection can make a thoroughly appropriable commodity of something so intangible as information. The very use of the information in any productive way is bound to reveal it, at least in part. Mobility of personnel among firms provides a way of spreading information. Legally imposed property rights can provide only a partial barrier, since there are obviously enormous difficulties in defining in any sharp way an item of information and differentiating it from other similar sounding items. The demand for information also has 55uncomfortable properties. . . . [T]here is a fundamental paradox in the determination of demand for information; its value for the purchaser is not known until he has the information, but then he has in effect acquired it without cost. Of course, if the seller can retain property rights in the use of the information, this would be no problem, but given incomplete appropriability, the potential buyer will base his decision to purchase information on less than optimal criteria. He may act, for example, on the average value of information in that class as revealed by past experience. If any particular item of information has differing values for different economic agents, this procedure will lead both to a nonoptimal purchase of information at any given price and also to a nonoptimal allocation of the information purchased.

———

As the foregoing excerpt notes, one way to solve both the free-rider problem and Arrow’s Information Paradox is through the adoption of laws to protect information even when it is shared. For example, early on, the grant of “royal favors” solved the free-rider problem in England by restricting who could publish books and other printed materials. But while this had the effect of making information available in printed form, it also limited competition and, therefore, the availability of information and the dissemination of knowledge. Also, by controlling supply, it drove up prices for printed material. Later, patent, copyright, and trade secret laws were devised to provide the developer of certain types of information with a degree of legal protection, but only in accordance with the limited scope of those rights.

One reason for the limited protection for information is the practical reality that “something so intangible as information” (to use Kenneth Arrow’s words) cannot be controlled absolutely (appropriated in economic terms). Thus, a lawyer and information professional who is charged with helping her client to protect its information should never rely upon “the law” alone. The law does not protect all information, and even if it did, the cost of enforcing such rights is beyond the means of some clients.

A second and related reason for the limits that are placed on the protection of information is more theoretical and focuses on the public policy choice of information diffusion, which is discussed at length in Chapter 3.

56

What Do You Think?

What might the internet look like today if Sir Tim Berners-Lee had not decided to dedicate the World Wide Web to the public? What if the use of popular internet services like Google and Facebook required paid membership? How might the lock-down of information and knowledge affect understanding, creativity, innovation, democracy and social interaction? Consider, for instance, the current market for scientific works.

Another way to solve the free-rider problem and Arrow’s Information Paradox involves an aspect of market regulation known as “private ordering” (primarily through contracts, the subject of Chapter 4). Private ordering is the process by which individuals and businesses voluntarily agree to order their private relationships. Although private ordering arrangements are often enforced by the law, they are generally thought to be outside of the realm of government regulation. In fact, many people who oppose government regulation cite private ordering as the preferred means of regulating private behavior.

The core idea of private ordering is that freely acting individuals and companies operating in a free market economy should be allowed to order their affairs as they wish. You can make a great deal, a bad deal, or a deal that you later regret (and under most circumstances, you cannot renege on a deal that you regret without paying damages). It is for this reason that “freedom to contract” is such a strong principle in the United States. But even private ordering has its limits, which will be discussed in more detail in Chapter 4 and elsewhere in this book. For now, it is enough to identify private ordering’s role in the information marketplace and for you to understand that contracting (often involving the licensing of rights in information) is a means to regulate the creation, collection, control, protection, and management of information, albeit primarily between the parties to a contract.

3.Architecture and Information

The term “architecture” refers to physical design, but not just to those physical structures that might be designed by architects and civil or mechanical engineers. More broadly, it refers to the design of tangible and intangible features of devices and spaces, including the design of communication technologies, computer systems, software, and the internet of things (IoT). As a means of regulating behavior, architecture (or design) can take many forms and may be both intentional and unintentional.
