493

Part III

Governance

■ ■ ■

If you have carefully read and considered Chapters 1 through 10, you have already learned the core of information law, including the definition of “information;” the theories that underlie information protection; the importance of information diffusion; and the laws that exist to require protection of certain information and that enable information to be protected or shared under specified conditions. In Chapter 7, you were also introduced to information security (InfoSec) and cybersecurity processes and frameworks. In Part III, you will learn about more information related laws as they arise and are applied in certain contexts and expand your understanding of the legal and practical issues that must be considered as part of an information management and security strategy.

We have titled this part of the book “governance” because it concerns how businesses should organize themselves to properly manage and secure the information they create, collect, use, and discard. In some circles, the terms “information security governance,” “data governance,” or “privacy governance” are used, but we prefer the more all-encompassing term “information governance” (IG) which Robert Smallwood described in his book, Information Governance: Concepts, Strategies, and Best Practices (Wiley 2014), as a “sort of super discipline.”

There are numerous IG definitions that have been developed by various organizations and individuals and, depending upon the definition, IG is often just a new name for the processes that InfoSec and cybersecurity professionals have been developing and following for decades. Indeed, despite the techy veneer, the practice of InfoSec and cybersecurity is more about process than technology. ARMA International (formerly the Association for Records Managers and Administrators (ARMA)), which has registered various IG-related trademarks and certification marks, defines IG as:

A strategic framework composed of standards, processes, roles, and metrics that hold organizations and individuals accountable to create, organize, secure, maintain, use, and dispose of information in ways that align with and contribute to the organization’s goals.

494

Consistent with the themes of this book (first introduced in Part I), we define IG as a holistic approach to information management that considers both legal and non-legal issues.

A simple way to understand the concept of IG is to consider four fundamental questions that are also at the heart of corporate governance: (1) How should the management of a business be organized?; (2) What are the roles and responsibilities of the various individuals and organizations within a business?; (3) What is the process for decisionmaking and the chain-of-authority for decisionmaking within the business?; and (4) How will responsible individuals and groups be monitored and held accountable? The implementation of IG requires companies to answer these and related questions with respect to the information that a company handles. While any IG structure within an institution should be a part of its broader governance structure, IG’s focus is on information related issues.

The IG process examines information practices from different perspectives and carefully considers the value and risks of information to its holder. This includes the “information dichotomy” between information protection (secrecy and privacy) and information diffusion and use. Awareness of the information dichotomy is important because, just as there are laws that require or facilitate information protection, there are laws that require or encourage information diffusion. Moreover, in the same way that there are benefits that companies can derive from information protection, there are benefits to be derived from information diffusion and use, often overlooked but necessitating a careful cost/benefit analysis.

A large part of the information governance (IG) process involves legal compliance and liability avoidance efforts, but it also involves a panoply of other business considerations. Thus, the most important thing to understand about IG is that it is a process, and not a fixed formula. It is akin to the practice of occupational safety and health management, but instead of focusing on the laws, regulations, and risks related to employee safety, it should focus on the laws, regulations, and risks associated with information.

IG requires a holistic approach because companies (and indeed, individuals) possess and handle different types of information, making a “one-size-fits-all” approach to information management and InfoSec undesirable. The IG strategy of a business, and how it is implemented, will depend upon a lot of different factors and, hopefully, it will evolve and improve over time.

In large part, the IG process is about changing the culture of a company so that every employee thinks about and understands the importance of information (as they should about workplace safety) in more sophisticated and sustained ways. Consultation and coordination between 495the direct managers and the custodians of the different types of information is required. This takes time and involves a lot of stakeholders. It is the job of information lawyers and information professionals to help their clients to develop and implement appropriate IG strategies and processes.

Within an organization, the IG process can involve: records and information management (RIM) professionals; computer scientists; information technology (IT) professionals; information security experts; database operators; privacy officers; cybersecurity experts; cloud computing providers; information technology providers; librarians; in-house and outside counsel; accountants; and auditors. It should also involve executive buy-in and oversight. This might involve common “C-level” executives such as: Chief Privacy Officer (CPO); Chief Information Security Officer (CISO); Data Protection Officer (DPO); Information Technology (IT) Directors; Chief Information Officers (CIO); and may include the Audit Committee of the Board of Directors of publicly-traded companies.

But the IG process should not just involve those employees who are hired for the specific purpose of information management or security (what we collectively call “information professionals”); an IG strategy should touch everyone who handles or uses information that is created or collected by a company or that flows through a company’s computer systems and information networks. Depending upon the nature of a company’s business, this could include information from employees, subcontractors, vendors, customers, and the public. It should also include supply-chain considerations; that is, the information and InfoSec practices of vendors and suppliers.

Part III begins in Chapter 11 with an overview of the IG process, which necessarily includes information security processes. Pay particular attention to the discussion of various frameworks and principles that have been developed to guide the IG process (but those, too, are still evolving). Chapters 12 through 16 examine applicable laws and information governance issues that arise in various contexts, including with respect to: corporations, litigation, government, national security, and law firms. In so doing, it models an approach to IG that can be used in other contexts and with respect to the associated laws and regulations.

We chose the topics covered in Chapters 12 through 16 not only because they involve interesting information related laws, but because they are likely to be of relevance to most information lawyers. Note, however, that there are numerous additional information related laws and regulations that apply to different aspects of a business or to different types of businesses, and we could have selected many other topics to discuss. For example, the laws and regulations governing the food industry, university technology transfer offices, and disability rights. Therefore, because there 496are numerous information laws and regulations that apply to a variety of different industries and situations, one of the first things information professionals should do as part of the IG process is conduct research to determine which information related laws and regulations apply in a given situation. Of course, information lawyers have an important role to play in this aspect of the IG process, as the following chapters illustrate.

﻿
497

Chapter 11

Information Governance

■ ■ ■

Anticipated Learning Outcomes

At the conclusion of this chapter, students should be able to: describe the general contours of the information governance process and the role of lawyers in that process; articulate the key principles of information governance; and outline an information governance plan.

Problem to consider as you read this chapter:

Imagine you are the Chief Intellectual Property (IP) Counsel for a major corporation, responsible for the protection and management of all of the company’s IP assets. Due to several strategic business considerations, the company decided to increase its trade secret and data protection efforts and has asked you to manage the project. Thus, you embark on a process of learning more about the information that the company owns, possesses, and handles, including the existing processes that are used to protect and manage that information (often referred to as an “information audit”).

Your company has done a great job implementing well-known trade secret protection measures (including employment policies, confidentiality agreements, noncompetition agreements, and security measures), but you learn that other information management processes within the company are lacking. For instance, although the company has a Chief Privacy Officer who does a great job protecting customers’ confidential personal information, there is no executive-level person who is charged with managing and protecting vendor, sub-contractor, and supply-chain information. Similarly, although the Corporate Secretary does a great job managing the corporate records of the company and has an extensive staff of records and information management professionals at her disposal, those record management efforts are not coordinated with other record management efforts within the company, for instance, with the Human Resources Department. As a result, there are inconsistencies in records management practices and different records management software and related security systems are in use that are managed by different Information Technology (IT) professionals. How would you go about improving the information management and security practices of your company?

498

A.Introduction

As further described below, information governance (IG) is about developing, implementing, monitoring, and improving a plan for the management and security of information in a dynamic everchanging environment. Thus, it is not unlike the practice of law. In the practice of law, lawyers are confronted with problems that they must solve while taking numerous factors into consideration, including their clients’ goals, the facts, and the law. Usually, the first step in this process is fact-gathering which, at the very least, should involve interviewing the client but often involves more sophisticated investigations. Next, the applicable law must be researched and evaluated to determine the client’s legal obligations and potential liability (or criminal responsibility). Once these two steps are completed, a plan of action for resolving the problem can be devised which can include both practical and legal solutions. Finally, the plan of action must to be implemented, monitored, evaluated and improved, as necessary.

Although still evolving and maturing, IG involves concepts from corporate governance, records management, IT governance, information security, data privacy, risk management, incident response, litigation readiness, regulatory compliance, and document storage and retention. It also includes related technologies, such as document management, enterprise search, knowledge management, and business continuity/disaster recovery. Part of IG concerns how a business is organized to manage information and how information related decisions are made. Generally, policies and procedures need to be established that allow a business to assess the value of, and risks posed by, the information it creates, collects, and uses.

Recall Professor Lessig’s four modalities of regulation that were described in Chapter 2: social norms; markets; architecture; and law. The IG process involves determining how best to utilize these four modalities to meet a business’ information management needs. As with most issues of this sort, including most legal problems, how the IG process meets a business’ information needs will depend upon the nature of the business and the context in which information related issues arise. Context matters because it determines the information that a client is likely to handle and the laws and legal obligations that apply to that information. But even without the existence of legal requirements, it is in the best interest of most companies (and individuals) to engage in good information practices.

A company’s executives will also be interested in the potential and actual value of information and the costs associated with its creation, collection, management, and protection, including potential liability for the mishandling of third-party information. Assessing these values and costs are part of the job of an IG lawyer also, and as the materials in this book 499demonstrate, this is not achievable without an understanding of a client’s business and information related objectives.

It is useful to think of the IG process as involving the entire lifecycle of information that is handled by an individual or business, from its creation or collection to its destruction, and including all uses and transmissions in-between. At each stage of the lifecycle of information, different values, risks, and legal obligations are likely to attach to different types of information. Ideally, some person or group of people within an organization will be charged with determining what those values, risks, and obligations are and how the information held by the organization will be handled as a result. But while certain individuals within a company may have a clear picture of the value, risks, and legal obligations associated with a discrete set of information (for instance, the Chief Privacy Officer with respect to the personal information of customers), the IG process requires a holistic approach. The virtue of such an approach is that it forces consideration of how the various information related goals and obligations of a company intersect with each other and other business goals and obligations and the extent to which they conflict or are complimentary.

The job of the lawyer is made easier by the fact that the law consists of numerous principles and analytical frameworks that help guide the factual and legal analysis and, thus, lawyers are used to utilizing these tools. For instance, the law of negligence directs lawyers to consider the issues of duty, breach, causation, and damages. The field of information management (or IG) has also developed numerous principles and frameworks that are designed to make the job of information professionals easier and more focused. Information lawyers and information professionals should become familiar with the IG principles and frameworks that are likely to apply to their clients, either because of the nature of their business or anticipated contractual requirements.

The principal components of the IG process and the involved individuals and groups within a business that should be concerned about IG are illustrated in the following framework known as the “Information Governance Reference Model” (IGRM), developed by EDRM (edrm.net) (which also developed the “Electronic Discovery Reference Model” that is discussed in Chapter 13).

500

Of course, knowing where information related issues arise and who is typically responsible for addressing them is only part of the IG story. The what, why, when, and how of a company’s IG needs must also be considered, necessitating a holistic approach to each listed IG issue.

501

What Do You Think?

When confronted with a new area of law, a new industry, or a new technology, and the new words and acronyms that accompany them, how would you go about learning what the words and acronyms mean? What sources of information would you consult and how would you verify the accuracy of the information you find? What if there are no fixed definitions yet? What if there is debate as to the proper definition? How would you decide what definitions best fit your client?

B.IG Principles and Frameworks

According to the online Business Dictionary, a framework is a: “Broad overview, outline, or skeleton of interlinked items which supports a particular approach to a specific objective, and serves as a guide that can be modified as required by adding or deleting items.” Different individuals and organizations (including both public and private organizations) have developed frameworks and principles for thinking about information and related IG and information security processes. For instance, earlier in this book (in Chapter 7) you were introduced to several “cybersecurity frameworks,” one developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and two others related to HIPAA and GLBA compliance. But there are others, including those created by private organizations, such as: (1) the ISO 27001 standard; (2) the SSAE18, third party risk standard; (3) HITRUST for use in the healthcare industry; (4) COSO, which is an auditing standard; and (5) COBIT v5, another auditing standard.

Frameworks are not immutable rules, rather they help to “frame” or guide processes. Thus, they serve as useful analytical devices; checklists of issues that should be considered with respect to a given objective. As so defined, different individuals and organization can have different views about the details of appropriate frameworks and associated processes, and information lawyers and information professionals are free to develop their own IG frameworks and processes or modify or supplement existing ones. In fact, it would be irresponsible for them not to do so if a suggested framework does not meet the needs of a client, for instance, with respect to the “reasonable security measures” that many clients are required to implement. In other words, information lawyers and other information professionals must exercise their independent judgement to determine whether compliance with a particular standard meets the needs of their clients. Indeed, this is the “value added” that information lawyers can bring to the IG process, and what clients will expect them to know.

Despite the need to exercise independent judgment, referring to existing IG frameworks and their underlying principles is always a good place to start the IG process. Moreover, there are at least four reasons why 502the use of particular policies and frameworks might be necessary: (1) some laws and regulations require or suggest that specific information related frameworks be used; (2) companies who seek assurances regarding information security will often insist that a particular framework be used; (3) many frameworks are designed to make the process of auditing and monitoring for compliance easier; and (4) specified frameworks may be designated by entities who grant information security and data protection certifications.

Most frameworks are based upon simple logic and common sense (like the I.R.A.C. framework of legal analysis), but they can also be structured around more detailed and sophisticated principles. As a baseline for our consideration of the IG process and IG frameworks, consider the following recordkeeping principles issued by ARMA International, which serves as a good starting point for our discussion of the IG process because they focus on information related issues. As you read the following principles, consider how the information dichotomy applies to each. Are the principles mainly about information protection or are there other concerns expressed?

ARMA International

Generally Accepted Recordkeeping Principles®

1.Principle of Accountability: A senior executive (or a person of comparable authority) shall oversee the information governance program and delegate responsibility for information management to appropriate individuals.

2.Principle of Transparency: An organization’s business processes and activities, including its information governance program, shall be documented in an open and verifiable manner, and that documentation shall be available to all personnel and appropriate, interested parties.

3.Principle of Integrity: An information governance program shall be constructed so the information assets generated by or managed for the organization have a reasonable guarantee of authenticity and reliability.

4.Principle of Protection: An information governance program shall be constructed to ensure an appropriate level of protection to information assets that are private, confidential, privileged, secret, classified, essential to business continuity, or that otherwise require protection.

5.Principle of Compliance: An information governance program shall be constructed to comply with applicable laws, other binding authorities, and the organization’s policies.

503

6.Principle of Availability: An organization shall maintain its information assets in a manner that ensures their timely, efficient, and accurate retrieval.

7.Principle of Retention: An organization shall maintain its information assets for an appropriate time, taking into account its legal, regulatory, fiscal, operational, and historical requirements.

8.Principle of Disposition: An organization shall provide secure and appropriate disposition for information assets no longer required to be maintained, in compliance with applicable laws and the organization’s policies.

While citing the foregoing principles with favor, and discussing them at length, Robert Smallwood developed a list of “ten key [IG] principles” which also incorporate the principles of confidentiality, integrity, and accessibility that were previously discussed in Chapters 6 through 8. They are: (1) executive sponsorship; (2) information policy development and communication; (3) information integrity; (4) information organization and classification; (5) information security; (6) information accessibility; (7) information control; (8) information governance monitoring and auditing; (9) stakeholder consultation; and (10) continuous improvement. See Robert F. Smallwood, Information Governance: Concepts, Strategies, and Best Practices (Wiley 2014).

What Do You Think?

Based upon the foregoing lists of IG principles, can you develop an IG framework? Where in the lifecycle of information do each of these principles arise and when should they be addressed? Which of the principles are likely to involve laws or regulations and which concern physical or cybersecurity?

C.Information Audits and Asset Registers

Generally, the purpose of an “information audit” is to gather facts about the information (in all formats) that a company owns, possesses, uses, and handles. This includes an assessment of both information per se and information technology (IT). Information lawyers and other information professionals can and should encourage their clients to conduct information audits that are designed to identify the information that they possess or own and that flows through the client’s computer systems and information networks. Only after an information audit is conducted can information lawyers and professionals engage in the necessary risk assessment and begin to give their clients comprehensive advice about the management and security of their information.

504

Logically and fundamentally, the first step in an IG process is fact-gathering. Here, one assesses the scope, nature, and uses of information that an organization possesses and handles. Thus, an information audit should begin by asking the appropriate people questions concerning the information that a client: (1) generates; (2) collects; (3) receives; (4) uses; (5) destroys; and (6) is obligated to or wishes to protect. Note that the identified information can take many forms (both tangible and intangible) and can come from a variety of sources, including employees, customers, vendors, consultants, and business partners. It can also flow in and out of a client’s business through multiple communication channels, including computer networks, the internet, mail services, the telephone, mobile devices, social media, and personal interactions. Moreover, the types of information that a company handles and collects can change over time, requiring regular updates to any existing IG plan.

Once identified, the information must be categorized according to its essential features, importance, and risks. Among other possible issues, consideration should be given to the following:

  • Nature of client’s business and industry: Does the client generate a lot of information, for instance, through research and development efforts or from customers? Does the client (or the industry in which it operates) prefer an open-innovation model of information exchange or a secretive model?
  • Ownership: Who owns the information? If it was generated by the client then it is likely to be owned by it (to the extent it can be owned), but issues of employee and third party ownership often arise. If the information was collected or received from third parties, then the client may not own the information, but only have a license to possess and use it. Is the information public domain information? Does the information qualify for intellectual property protection and, if so, who owns those rights?
  • Use: How and where is the information used? Is it shared with others outside of the company? Is it essential to the client’s business or of ancillary importance? Who needs to use and access the information?
  • Access and control: Who has access to the information? Is access restricted and, if so, by what means? Do any contractual obligations regarding access and control apply to the information?
  • Confidential status: Is the information public or confidential? If confidential, to what extent is it also trade 505secret information? Is the information generally known or readily ascertainable?
  • Protection and Security: What steps have been taken to protect and secure the information? Have the users of the information, and those who have access to it, been required to sign a confidentiality agreement? Have employees been informed of their obligations with respect to company information? If so, how? What physical and cybersecurity measures are being used to secure the information?
  • Nature and type: What is the nature of the information? Is the information a form of intellectual property? Is it the type of information that is subject to laws governing its handling and security, such as privacy laws? Was the information received from a third party subject to a duty of confidentiality? Is the information historical records or archival information that should or must be kept?
  • Potential risks and liability: Might the possession or use of the information expose the client to potential liability, for instance, for data breach, trade secret misappropriation, or breach of contract?
  • Storage and flow: Where and how is the information kept and stored and for how long? If it is maintained digitally, on which computer systems is it stored? Is it stored on internal servers or in the cloud? Where and how is the information accessed and transmitted?
  • Retention: Is the retention of the information necessary and, if so, for how long? Do legal or contractual requirements for the storage and retention of the information apply? Is the information relevant to threatened or ongoing litigation?
  • Value: What is the veracity and value of the information? Is it worth expending money to protect and secure? Can the company derive revenue from the information?

Based upon the answers to the foregoing questions a classification scheme for the client’s information can be devised and a comprehensive IG plan can be developed.

Broadly, the identified information should be classified according to whether the client: (1) wishes to protect the information pursuant to applicable self-help, contract, and tort principles; (2) must protect the information pursuant to applicable law or contractual obligations; or (3) does not need to protect (or, perhaps, even keep) the information and should destroy it or return it to its owner. At a more granular level, each “information set” will be labeled with a distinct name and assigned rules 506and policies for its handling. For instance, one information set might be labeled “personal customer information,” while another is labeled “trade secrets.” To keep the classification scheme manageable, it is often recommended that only 3–4 classifications be devised, such as: (1) public; (2) confidential; and (3) sensitive.

So-called “unstructured information” (largely, daily correspondence and communications in the form of emails, texts, and social media postings) must also be accounted for and classified. However, the information that is collected by a business may also be maintained and used in ways that makes its segregation into different information (or data) sets difficult, thereby often requiring an IG approach that treats all information in that information set in accordance with the most important or sensitive information.

Recalling the Generally Accepted Recordkeeping Principles and audit questions above, among other possible issues that should be addressed in IG rules and policies are: (1) who is responsible for the management of the information (often labeled the “owner” for internal purposes); (2) where and how the information will be stored; (3) where and how the information is used; and (4) who will be allowed to access and use the information. As further discussed in chapters that follow, appropriate policies and procedures for retaining, sharing, and discarding information should also be devised, including policies and procedures for the proper use and disposal of the devices that store information.

Once an IG strategy is developed and implemented, regular audits and monitoring are an important means of ensuring that established IG policies and processes are being followed. (Article 35 of the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) requires a Data Privacy Impact Assessment (DPIA).) To that end, note that these audits and assessments (or inventories) should not be confused with external audits of company functions that are required by various laws, including the “data protection audits” that supervisory authorities are empowered to conduct pursuant to Article 58.1(b) of the GDPR. Whereas information audits are performed by individuals and companies to determine the amount and types of information they possess, external audits are performed by third parties or regulatory authorities to determine if a company is meeting its obligations under applicable law. As the regulation of information increases, one can expect that external information related audits and oversight (including of information security and data protection practices) will become more common.

Related to the information audit is the “asset register,” the creation of which is a critical part of the information security and IG processes. It is a record (often kept in the form of a spreadsheet) that records the information related assets of a business. It should include a listing of the 507information identified as part of an information audit, as well as an inventory of a company’s information technology (IT) related assets, including: (1) hardware; (2) software; (3) communications infrastructure; (4) information contracts and licenses; (5) outsourced services; and (6) information related personnel. Typically, the asset register will indicate who within a company is responsible for each asset (“the owner”), who is the custodian of each asset, and where the asset is located.

D.Researching the Applicable Law

An important (some might say crucial) part of the IG process is to determine the legal obligations that attach to the information that a company possesses and handles, including whether a given company is required to create, keep, or record specified documents. (The primary existing laws were discussed in Part II of this book.) Understanding legal obligations serves at least three purposes: (1) legal compliance; (2) risk assessment and management; and (3) information protection.

Generally, what constitutes “applicable law” with respect to a given set of information will depend upon two facts: (1) the identity of the information; and (2) the applicable jurisdiction. For instance, if the identified information is comprised of the personal information of residents of California and the European Union, at least three separate sets of laws are implicated: California’s privacy laws; the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR); and U.S. federal law. If the information includes the personal information of residents of other states or countries, then those laws must be considered as well. Similarly, if the subject information was created by a company and is therefore owned by it, there are a variety of different laws that the company might use to protect that information, including patent, copyright, contract, and trade secret laws.

Another way to find applicable information related laws and regulations is through an industry or sector-specific approach. In this regard, it is important to understand that the legal obligations that one company has with respect to its information may be vastly different from the obligations that are imposed on a company in a different industry. This may be because the information that one company handles is more sensitive than the information of another company; for instance, if the information is the subject of national security concerns (discussed in Chapter 15) or constitutes “protected health information” subject to HIPAA (discussed in Chapters 6 and 7). Or it may be because of the different information sharing norms and practices of a client or the industry in which it operates. Some clients may prefer an open innovation model of conducting business that requires the free-flow of certain bodies of information, while others may prefer strict confidentiality.

508

There are many information related laws and regulations that may apply depending upon the nature of a client’s business and the types of information it possesses and handles, and, as was discussed in Chapter 4, often information related legal obligations are imposed by contract. The ability to find and analyze applicable law is the province of all lawyers, making the information lawyer a critical part of any IG process. Chapters 12 through 16 that follow provide additional information about information related laws in various contexts and further insights about where to look for applicable law.

E.Developing and Implementing an IG Strategy

Once one is aware of the information that a company owns, possesses, and handles and understands the laws and regulations that apply to that information, the next step in the IG process is to develop an IG strategy and implementation plan that is consistent with the mission and values of the company. This is where consideration of the information dichotomy arises once again. Sometimes the principal mission of a company is to create, collect, and protect information, and sometimes it is to disseminate and share information. Often, companies pursue both missions simultaneously, but with respect to different bodies of information. Of course, a large part of any IG strategy should include an information security plan and related policies and procedures. (Recall the NIST Cybersecurity Framework discussed in Chapter 7.)

There are various necessary components to an IG strategy, but how it is ultimately designed and implemented depends upon several organization-specific factors. First, there is the human component: Who will be involved in the IG process and, most importantly, who will be held accountable for its implementation? Accountability is a critical aspect of any business strategy, and no IG strategy should be designed without at least one high-level person being designated to oversee its implementation. Many proponents of IG practices assert that companies should appoint a “Chief Information Governance Officer” to oversee a company’s IG strategy, but it is the functions of the job, and not the title, that really matter. The key is to have executive buy-in, support, and oversight.

Anyone who delves into the world of information technology, information management, privacy, and security will quickly realize that titles, certifications, frameworks, principles, best practices, and acronyms abound. When hiring information professionals and assigning titles, companies are generally free to use whatever titles they wish and, thus, numerous information related titles and job descriptions exist even though job responsibilities are often the same. It can be quite confusing and intimidating, particularly when those in the field speak in acronym-based 509code. IG lawyers need to understand the roles and interests of all the information professionals that work for a company, whatever their titles or chosen acronyms (RIM, IT, InfoSec, CISO, etc.). This includes the norms, best practices, and standards of those professionals and the core principles that should guide the management and handling of the information under their charge.

Second, one must consider the company’s goals and objectives. The underlying presumption is that no IG strategy should be developed without an understanding of the culture of the company and potential practical and sociological barriers to successfully implementing the strategy. Among the questions to consider: What does the company hope to gain from an IG strategy? Is the principal concern legal compliance and risk management, or does the company also wish to gain value from its information? Is there potential value in digitizing and monetizing a company’s information? If so, what are the risks and costs associated with doing so? How does the organization’s existing culture take these issues into account, if at all? If a company is built upon an open innovation model, can information protection measures be improved upon or managed? Related to this and the first component: Who is responsible for determining IG policies? Without an IG strategy, individual units of a company that are responsible for managing certain aspects of a company’s information are certain to develop policies and procedures, but who is examining how those various policies and procedures interact and whether they are consistent with the business objectives of the company?

Development of an IG strategy should begin with a formal and comprehensive risk assessment, particularly with respect to the security of information and related information technology (IT) systems. This is due to the dynamic nature of information within the information ecosystem. In contrast to the pre-internet era, the advent of the internet and related devices, including smart phones and the internet of things (IoT), has exponentially increased the risks posed to the security of information. Gone are the days when static information was stored away in a box that was seldom accessed by company employees. Today, information management requires a risk assessment of: every place and device where information is used and stored; every device by which information is transmitted; and all transmission networks in between. This will necessarily involve the expertise of IT and computer security professionals, either in-house employees or outside consultants, and an examination of all applicable hardware, middleware, and software applications.

The risk assessment should also include an analysis of current information and security practices to determine their strengths and weaknesses and how they might be improved with respect to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability (CIA) of a company’s information. Consideration must be given to: (1) the threats posed to the 510information; (2) actual or potential vulnerabilities; and (3) the likely impact of the threats and vulnerabilities. Once actual and potential risks are identified, decisions must be made about how to address or manage those risks through: (1) remediation; (2) avoidance; (3) mitigation; (4) transfer; or (5) acceptance.

Although companies should comply with all applicable laws and regulations and avoid potential liability where possible, how they do so should be based upon a cost/benefit analysis. This assessment should consider the value of the information to a company, the potential legal consequences and other losses associated with the information, the probability of the risk occurring, and the cost of remediation or other measures. Some laws and regulations may give a company little choice but to institute specified measures but often they only require “reasonable” efforts, and what is reasonable depends upon the circumstances.

Risk assessments are often conducted using a “risk matrix” where identified risks are ranked in accordance with their likelihood and severity of impact, thereby allowing companies to focus on the most significant risks first. Where a company does not have the financial resources to institute a comprehensive IG strategy, choices will have to be made.

Legal obligations alone should not dictate whether a company keeps, uses, or destroys the information it possesses. An organization will also want to consider broader operational, financial, strategic, and cultural concerns. For instance, consideration must be given to the information that the company’s employees need to effectively and efficiently perform their work. Also, there may be ancillary reasons to keep information. For instance: Is the information of potential historical or marketing significance? Or, might the retention of the information prove to be favorable evidence in a future lawsuit, for instance, to prove that the company did not pollute a nearby river?

With respect to digitized information, an examination of the policies, procedures, and staffing of the IT department, including a review of existing computer infrastructure and software, must be conducted. Such examination should include an exploration and inventory of existing physical and cybersecurity efforts and tools (referred to as “controls” among InfoSec and cybersecurity experts). As explained by Charlotte Tschider in her book, International Cybersecurity and Privacy Law in Practice (Wolters Kluwer 2017): “In order to build an effective information security program, attorneys and practitioners should understand an organization’s existing governance processes, both related to IT and to other parts of an organization.”

Specific policies and practices that should be examined (and created if they do not already exist) will address such issues as: (1) asset management, including physical assets (such as laptops and mobile 511phones) and virtual assets (such as management of IT application, utility, and infrastructure lifecycles); (2) information technology management (hardware, middleware, and software); (3) threat assessment and monitoring; (4) risk management, including software vulnerabilities; (5) cybersecurity; (6) physical security; (7) social media use; (8) data classification, retention and destruction; (9) privacy and confidentiality; (10) identity and access management, including password and encryption policies; and (11) incident response, including data breach notification.

A critical part of any IG plan is the development of written policies and procedures and related agreements. Common policies address: access and use; encryption; information classification; privacy; acceptable use; mobile device; removable media; incident response; social media; physical security; and information use and sharing. Particular attention should be paid to the policies and agreements governing third parties who are allowed to access and use company information, including supply-side vendors. Consideration must also be given to the costs of implementation, in terms of money and other factors, like employee morale and public and customer relations. This is where the risk management aspects of the IG planning process play a crucial role.

As was previously discussed in Part II of this book, particularly Chapter 4, the implementation of an IG strategy is likely to involve the use of contracts. For instance, a company that seeks to protect a company’s confidential, proprietary, and trade secret information should develop policies and contracts for the protection of specified information. Typically, this would take the form of company policies coupled with confidentiality or nondisclosure agreements (NDAs), but it might also include noncompetition, non-solicitation, and invention assignment agreements. Contracts, usually in the form of privacy policies, terms of use (or service) agreements, and license agreements, can also be used to limit a company’s liability for its misuse of customer and vendor information. Other strategies to limit such liability include: (1) data minimization (not collecting the information in the first instance); or (2) destroying the information once it is no longer needed, provided that doing so is consistent will applicable law.

A related part of the IG process concerns the lexicon of the various information management fields and the associated technology. To harmonize terminology within a given organization, companies should insist upon common definitions of the terms and acronyms used, thereby reducing definitional confusion. If there is no common definition for a term, they should be careful to define terms in all pertinent policies and contracts. The need for clear definitions seems obvious, but it is more pronounced and challenging than one may realize. For starters, although one would hope that common IT and IG definitions exist, this is not always the case, particularly involving technological advances.

512

Next, an IG implementation plan must be developed, preferably to include performance benchmarks and audits (internal and external) and regular monitoring of information use. In this regard, it is important to develop an IG plan with future audits and performance evaluations in mind, meaning that the question of compliance with applicable rules and polices can be answered with a “yes” or “no” answer. Thus, although a law might only require “reasonable efforts to maintain secrecy” or “reasonable cybersecurity precautions,” the rules and policies of a company’s IG plan should be more specific so that a “yes” or “no” answer can be given. For instance, the plan might require all visitors to be signed-in and issued a visitor’s badge so that an information audit can assess whether these specific requirements were met.

Published privacy and security frameworks can be helpful in identifying potential performance benchmarks as they often state what should be done in a given situation, for instance, “X” information shall be encrypted or access to “Y” database shall require two-factor authentication. But just because a framework specifies certain steps to be taken does not mean that the implementation of those steps will be deemed “reasonable” in a court of law. Moreover, the nature of a client’s business and the information it keeps may require it to institute policies and procedures that exceed what a private or governmental organization deems reasonable.

The development of an IG strategy is meaningless if it is not known or followed. Thus, education and training are important parts of IG implementation. This is particularly important with respect to information privacy and security since many sensitive information breaches have occurred due to the failure of employees to follow basic information security and trade secret policies. Companies have been known to spend millions of dollars on sophisticated cybersecurity software and monitoring, only to suffer a data breach due to a low-level employee clicking on an attachment in a “phishing” email that allowed a hacker to gain access to a company’s computer system or using a corrupted USB drive. Or, a company’s information has been lost because the data encryption policy it adopted was not followed.

By analogy to occupational health and safety policies, developing IG policies and procedures but failing to educate employees about them would be like requiring construction workers to wear hardhats in high-risk areas but then never explaining what is considered a high-risk area or providing hardhats. To implement an IG strategy, employees and third parties must first be given both the knowledge and tools that they need to comply with published policies. In addition to being educated about the applicable rules and policies, they need to be taught the applicable analytical process: (1) what is the information to be protected; (2) what laws, if any, apply to the subject information; (3) what company policies, if any, apply to the subject information; and (4) what do the applicable laws and policies require? The 513same series of questions can be asked with respect to the various physical devices that are used by employees or provided to third party vendors.

An important aspect of any IG strategy should involve regular monitoring of information use and access. Computer “hacking,” for instance, can usually be spotted using data analytics that examine data usage patterns, both company-wide and with respect to specific databases and computers. Similarly, it is possible to monitor who and when someone gains access to a database. Here again, however, these techniques will not work effectively unless the policies that require monitoring are followed and the employees who are charged with the monitoring have the knowledge and tools they need to perform their responsibilities.

Also, breaches of policies and protocols may occur that cannot be monitored by sophisticated computer software and data analytics; for instance, when an employee with proper access to a database allows his password and encryption key to be seen or used by others. (See the discussion of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act in Chapter 9). The possibility of human failings means that the implementation of an IG strategy should seek to alter the culture of a business so that the proper handling and management of information becomes second nature and so that security and privacy policies and procedures are understood and followed.

Of course, given the mass digitization of information and the widespread use of the internet and cloud computing services, the implementation of an IG strategy will involve technological approaches and solutions. This is where the expertise of computer scientists and information technology (IT) specialists is critical. But given the potential costs of technical approaches, an IG plan should also consider how IT costs and cybersecurity risks can be minimized by reducing the amount of information a company receives, processes, and maintains. In other words: what is the company’s “data minimization” strategy? Adopting a data minimization approach is likely to require the IT department to expand its thinking and processes to consider strategies for information reduction, as well as for information storage, flow, and security. A potential side benefit of a data minimization strategy is that there will be less potentially relevant documents to produce during litigation.

Finally, an IG plan should include a process for periodic assessment and reevaluation, particularly given the evolutionary nature of the information ecosystem and the technology that supports it. Usually, these would be conducted at least annually, but circumstances might require more frequent assessments. Also, while a comprehensive assessment should be conducted annually, assessments of individual components of an IG plan might be scheduled on a rotating basis throughout the year. IG plan assessments and reevaluations are particularly important when a 514company expands its products or services or acquires another company. Of course, an examination of the information management practices of the company being acquired should be a part of the due diligence process.

The ARMA principles and information audit questions above provide a great list of the information related issues that should be considered as part of the process of developing an IG plan and strategy and suggest numerous information related goals and objectives that a company may wish to adopt. But there are other lists of principles, frameworks, and best practices that could provide critical insights. For instance, the cybersecurity laws and frameworks that are discussed in Chapter 7 should be consulted with respect to information security issues. As discussed in Chapter 13, the laws and frameworks related to e-discovery should also be considered. Additionally, the insights and expertise of the various information professionals (RIM, IT, librarians, archivists, etc.) who are involved in the management of a company’s information should be part of all decisions regarding information assets.

In closing, and as discussed at the beginning of this chapter, a primary purpose of an IG approach to information management is to change the culture of an organization so that information management and security is a top concern. But this focus can be easily misunderstood. For instance, employees can easily be led to believe that they must protect “all” of an organization’s information, when that is not the objective of the subject IG plan. Or they may believe that every document they generate must be encrypted, when that is not company policy. Such overbreadth can lead to the use of limited company resources for little or no payoff and could be potentially harmful by unduly limiting access to and the use of information. A holistic approach to IG, and a granular understanding of a client’s information needs and risks, will create in clients a respect for information management that may very well have been unrecognized and underappreciated before the IG process was implemented.

Notes

1.Technological competence. Part of the job of an information professional, including information lawyers, is to become “technologically competent.” In fact, the American Bar Association (ABA) Model Rules of Professional Conduct, Rule 1.1 requires that “a lawyer should keep abreast of the law and its practice, including the benefits and risks associated with relevant technology, engage in continuing study and education and comply with all continuing legal education requirements to which the lawyer is subject.” (Emphasis added.) While this does not require information lawyers to become experts in computer science and information technology, it does require them to understand basic principles, such as: common protection measures like passwords, encryption, and dual-factor authentication; and common threats, including computer hacking, phishing, and denial of service (DOS) attacks. 515Information lawyers and professionals should also keep informed about available technological products and solutions for the management of information. Many computer and high-tech companies provide IG products and services and, as with IG processes generally, these products and services are bound to evolve and improve over time.
